KEY MESSAGE 1...
A Frost Advisory remains up to 9 am for southeast Warren and 
Washington Counties for areas of frost forming as temps fall 
into the mid 30s. The strong anticyclone centered over southern 
Quebec has produced ideal radiational cooling conditions for 
lows to fall into the 30s and lower 40s. Some patchy to areas of
locally dense fog have formed along the CT River Valley, 
Mohawk-Hudson Valley juncture and the Upper Hudson River Valley 
towards Lake George. The mist/fog should burn off quickly after 
shortly after sunrise. 

Another dry and cool day is expected with abundant sunshine with
the strong surface high in control. Max temps were accepted
close to the NBM highs with mid and upper 60s in the valleys and
mid 50s to lower 60s over the higher terrain which are still
below normal. Some radiational cooling is expected tonight, but
high clouds will begin to increase at night. Lows were lowered 
closer to a NBM/ADJMAV/CONSMOS blend with lows in the mid 30s to
lower 40s north and west of the Greater Capital Region and 
mainly lower to mid 40s to the south and east. Some patchy fog 
may form again in some of the river and sheltered valleys.
Clouds increase on Friday, and PoPs were reduced to just a
slight or low chance late in the day for the mid Hudson
Valley/Berkshires and NW CT, as they would be associated with 
an inverted sfc trough to developing oceanic cyclone well south 
and east of the Delmarva Region. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...
The oceanic/coastal low makes slow progress lifting 
north/northwest in the western Atlantic Fri night through Sun. 
Several ensemble members, deterministic medium range solutions 
and AI have the storm approaching southeast New England and 
eastern Long Island Friday night into Saturday bringing periods 
of showers in the deformation zone or northwest quadrant of the 
potent low. The cyclone may then move over southeast New England
and loop around going over or south of the Long Island for the 
2nd half of the weekend with periods of rain and some gusty 
winds. Confidence remains high for this storm to bring rainfall, 
but subtle shifts in the track and timing are likely to continue
due to the strong blocking high to the north keeping this 
system surpressed. In fact the latest EC/AI-EC has this storm 
only just east of the Mid Atlantic Region by Saturday morning 
and lifting north and backing westward south of Long Island and 
moving into NJ Sat night into Sunday. Our forecast leans closer 
to the northern most solutions of the GEFS/AI-GFS/GFS/CMC and 
some of the EC ensembles which is exhibited by the NBM.

The timing and track issues keeps confidence low to moderate at
best in terms of impacts from rainfall and wind. Bands of
showers rotating around the wave are expected Sat-Sun across
eastern NY and western New England. PWATs run above normal.
Clouds will keep temps cooler than normal on Sat and possibly
Sunday. The wave may sit and spin over southern New England or
be just south of Long Island, while it meanders and loops 
around late Sat into Mon. In fact, scattered showers may persist
into Monday now. Some drier weather may return by Tue.

The probabilities for rainfall are greatest in the 60-80% range
from the northern Catskills, Greater Capital Region and southern
VT south and east Sat through Sun. Again, the track and
evolution of the system may vary the timing of the rain showers
and possibly a few thunderstorms that could pop up on Sunday. 
The rainfall does not like problematic at this point with the 
recent dry antecedent conditions. The latest NBM 48-hr probs > 
1" of rainfall for the period ending 8 am Mon are 30-50% along a
northern/eastern Catskills, Greater Capital Region and southern
VT axis south and east with the highest probs over NW CT. NBM 
probs >2" are only 20-25% for the same time frame for NW CT and 
less than 15% elsewhere. Some ponding of water may occur with 
any heavier showers/poor drainage flooding of low-lying area. 
WPC has expanded the Marginal Risk in the Day 3 ERO from Albany 
south and east. North/northeast winds increase on the 
west/northwest side of the storm Fri night through Sat night, 
as the horizontal sfc pressure gradient increases. The 24-hr NBM
probs > 35 mph wind gusts are mainly over the eastern 
Catskills, northern Taconics, Berkshires, NW CT and the mid 
Hudson Valley for the time period ending 2 am Sunday. These same
areas excluding the mid Hudson River Valley for the period 
ending 2 am Sunday for wind gusts > 40 mph, the probs lower to 
20-40% and fall below 15% for gusts > 45 mph. Some foliated 
tree limbs could be downed, but the gusts at this point fall 
short of Wind Advisory criteria (46-57 mph), but will continue 
to be monitored. The winds should subside by Sunday into Sunday 
night. Overall, impacts look limited at this time.
